newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope says media interested in money not values.
newsitem.headline: Pope says media interested in money not values.

text.p: Pope John Paul said on Friday that Western media organisations exporting their products around the world were more interested in making profits than spreading appropriate cultural values.

In his written message for the Roman Catholic Church's World Communications Day, the Pope also said high-tech media were making it ever more difficult for parents to guard their children from unwholesome messages entering their homes.
Without mentioning them specifically he also appeared to back moves to protect minors by passing laws to limit what can be transmitted on television or on the Internet.

"In some parts of the world voices are being raised against what is seen as domination of the media by so-called Western culture. Media products are seen as in some way representing values that the West holds dear, and by implication, they supposedly present Christian values," the Pope said.
"The truth of the matter may well be that the foremost value they genuinely represent is commercial profit," he said.
People who wanted to use the media to spread good were not seizing the new opportunities available to them, he added.
The Pope said public opinion had been shocked by how easily advanced communication technologies could be exploited by those "whose intentions are evil".
This was an apparent reference to recent reports in Europe about paedophiles using the Internet global computer network to distribute child pornography.
The Pope also appeared to be referring to worries by parents who want to protect their children from unwanted images or messages, particularly via cable television and the Internet.
"The fact is that it is increasingly difficult to protect one's eyes and ears from images and sounds which arrive through the media unexpectedly and uninvited," the Pope said.

"It is particularly hard for parents to guard their children from unwholesome messages, and to ensure that their education in human relations and their learning about the world comes about in a way that is appropriate to their age and sensibility."
The issue is particularly topical in the United States, where the Supreme Court has agreed to decide on a landmark case on the right to free speech in cyberspace.
The U.S. high court is due to hear a Justice Department appeal seeking to reinstate a federal law that effectively bans indecent material on the Internet.

Backed by President Bill Clinton, the Justice Department last year asked the court to overturn a precedent-setting ruling in June by three federal judges in Philadelphia declaring unconstitutional key parts of the Communications Decency Act.

The law, signed by Clinton a year ago as part of a telecommunications overhaul, bars the distribution to minors of indecent or "patently offensive" materials on the Internet, which is used by an estimated 40 million people.
